title: Six Lights
concept: Read six DSCP lights without confusing the two ECN lights.

briefing.title: Six Lights
briefing.explanation: DSCP occupies the upper six bits; PHB selection uses the entire six-bit codepoint and ignores the lower two bits. The lower two bits are the ECN field: 00 Not-ECT, 01 ECT(1), 10 ECT(0), 11 CE.
briefing.example: Read six DSCP lights without confusing the two ECN lights.
simplifications: Crates stand for packets; shipping labels stand for packet fields and application identity.
Time advances in fixed ticks. Traffic traces do not react to loss.
Belts add one tick per grid tile; factory geometry is a teaching metaphor.
briefing.plain_language: Every voice crate carries the same lane label: DSCP 46. One sorter rule is looking for 47 instead. Make that small correction and watch both voice crates take the voice lane.

wrong-route.why_wrong: The BA sorter compares the wrong six-bit value. ECN does not change which PHB the DSCP selects.
wrong-route.concept_reinforced: Read six DSCP lights without confusing the two ECN lights.

hints.text: Separate the two smaller ECN lights from the six DSCP lights.
The six weights are 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. Add only the lit DSCP weights.
The two voice crates have different ECN bits. Their six-bit DSCP values still match.

title: Codepoint Forge
concept: Make named DSCPs with six bit toggles.

briefing.title: Codepoint Forge
briefing.explanation: Class Selector codepoints have the form xxx000; CSx is therefore 8 times x. The twelve AF codepoints correspond to AFxy = 8x + 2y for x=1..4 and y=1..3. The recommended EF codepoint is binary 101110, decimal 46.
briefing.example: Make named DSCPs with six bit toggles.
simplifications: Crates stand for packets; shipping labels stand for packet fields and application identity.
Time advances in fixed ticks. Traffic traces do not react to loss.
Belts add one tick per grid tile; factory geometry is a teaching metaphor.
briefing.plain_language: A marker changes the six DSCP lights. Use their weights to make each requested codepoint. The two smaller ECN lights are preserved automatically.

wrong-mark.why_wrong: The paint booth produces a different DSCP from the named target. A nearby binary value is a different codepoint.
wrong-mark.concept_reinforced: Make named DSCPs with six bit toggles.

hints.text: CS codepoints end with three zero bits.
AF class and drop precedence occupy different parts of the six-bit value.
Use the codepoint formula in the briefing, then express the result as six bit weights.

title: The Old Sorter
concept: Predict what only the upper three bits reveal.

briefing.title: The Old Sorter
briefing.explanation: Legacy IP Precedence reads the upper three bits; it cannot distinguish AF41 from AF43, EF from CS5, or AF11 from CS1.
briefing.example: Predict what only the upper three bits reveal.
simplifications: Crates stand for packets; shipping labels stand for packet fields and application identity.
Time advances in fixed ticks. Traffic traces do not react to loss.
Belts add one tick per grid tile; factory geometry is a teaching metaphor.
briefing.plain_language: This old sorter reads only the first three DSCP lights. Different six-bit labels can look the same to it. Predict which p0, p1, p4 or p5 dock each crate reaches.

wrong-prediction.why_wrong: At least one predicted dock differs from the three-bit precedence route computed by the engine.
wrong-prediction.concept_reinforced: Predict what only the upper three bits reveal.

hints.text: Read only the first three of the six DSCP lights.
Compare AF41 with AF43, then EF with CS5.
The old sorter cannot recover information from bits it does not read.

title: Who Goes Where
concept: Classify the shipping label, then mark the service class.

briefing.title: Who Goes Where
briefing.explanation: BA classification uses DSCP; MF classification uses combinations of header fields and other information such as incoming interface. A marker assigns a DS codepoint, possibly based on meter state; changing the codepoint is re-marking. RFC 4594 recommends EF for the Telephony service class. RFC 4594 recommends CS5 for the Signaling service class. RFC 4594 recommends AF41/AF42/AF43 for the Multimedia Conferencing service class. RFC 4594 recommends CS4 for the Real-Time Interactive service class. RFC 4594 recommends AF31/AF32/AF33 for the Multimedia Streaming service class. RFC 4594 recommends CS3 for the Broadcast Video service class. RFC 4594 recommends AF21/AF22/AF23 for the Low-Latency Data service class. RFC 4594 recommends CS2 for the OAM service class. RFC 4594 recommends AF11/AF12/AF13 for the High-Throughput Data service class. RFC 4594 recommends DF for the Standard service class.
briefing.example: Classify the shipping label, then mark the service class.
simplifications: Crates stand for packets; shipping labels stand for packet fields and application identity.
Time advances in fixed ticks. Traffic traces do not react to loss.
Belts add one tick per grid tile; factory geometry is a teaching metaphor.
briefing.plain_language: The shipping label tells you what the application is. The sorter already separates the applications; set each paint booth to the recommended service label.

wrong-mark.why_wrong: The VoIP label does not match its intended MF rule, so its marker produces the wrong service-class DSCP.
wrong-mark.concept_reinforced: Classify the shipping label, then mark the service class.

hints.text: Read the shipping-label application before choosing a route.
MF rules are tested in order; the first match selects the output.
The marker on a route assigns the service-class DSCP. The marker and classifier are separate elements.

title: Trust Boundary
concept: Accept a trusted routing mark; re-mark untrusted claims.

briefing.title: Trust Boundary
briefing.explanation: RFC 4594 recommends CS6 for Network Control and dropping or re-marking untrusted CS6 at ingress. RFC 4594 recommends CS6 for routing/control, reserves CS7 for possible future control use, and excludes user traffic from Network Control treatment. A marker assigns a DS codepoint, possibly based on meter state; changing the codepoint is re-marking.
briefing.example: Accept a trusted routing mark; re-mark untrusted claims.
simplifications: Crates stand for packets; shipping labels stand for packet fields and application identity.
Time advances in fixed ticks. Traffic traces do not react to loss.
Belts add one tick per grid tile; factory geometry is a teaching metaphor.
briefing.plain_language: A trusted router may use a routing label. A user device cannot grant itself that privilege. Clear the six DSCP lights on the untrusted remark booth.

untrusted-mark.why_wrong: The untrusted lane still delivers a network-control marking. Changing CS7 to CS6 does not remove its privileged claim.
untrusted-mark.concept_reinforced: Accept a trusted routing mark; re-mark untrusted claims.

hints.text: The source dock defines trust; the crate cannot declare itself trusted.
Only the untrusted path needs its control marking removed.
A marker changes the six DSCP bits while preserving the two ECN bits.

title: The Water Tower
concept: Spend tokens to keep voice within its contract.

briefing.title: The Water Tower
briefing.explanation: A meter compares packet timing against a traffic profile and supplies state to conditioning actions. Dropping traffic to bring it into compliance with a profile is policing. RFC 4594 recommends policing EF traffic to protect the network and providing low-delay service.
briefing.example: Spend tokens to keep voice within its contract.
simplifications: Crates stand for packets; shipping labels stand for packet fields and application identity.
Time advances in fixed ticks. Traffic traces do not react to loss.
Belts add one tick per grid tile; factory geometry is a teaching metaphor.
Output docks can accept the whole burst; these lessons isolate metering from output congestion.
Token buckets begin full. Refill is exact to whole bytes; sub-byte credit is retained.
briefing.plain_language: The tank is a spending limit. Each byte needs one token. Green means the crate fits; red means it exceeds the allowance. First predict the fixed tank, then repair the editable tank below.

unpoliced-priority.why_wrong: The configured rate exceeds the voice contract, so the burst flood is admitted instead of being policed.
unpoliced-priority.concept_reinforced: Spend tokens to keep voice within its contract.

hints.text: A token pays for one byte. The bucket starts full.
The fixed prediction tank holds 1000 bytes and refills at 1000 bytes per second.
For the build, match the 1000 B/s contract and a 1000-byte burst. Keep the excess lane connected to the Recycler.

guide: Predict the fixed tank: 1000 B/s, burst 1000 bytes.
Select tank and set its rate and burst to the contract values.
Run both parts. Only a pass on both completes the work order.

title: Cascade
concept: One refill stream, two buckets, three colors.

briefing.title: Cascade
briefing.explanation: srTCM starts full, refills committed then excess at CIR, and tests entire packet size against committed then excess tokens. In color-aware srTCM, a precolored yellow packet cannot become green and a red packet remains red. srTCM uses CIR in bytes per second and CBS/EBS in bytes; at least one bucket size must be positive. RFC 4594 recommends srTCM and AF21/AF22/AF23 for Low-Latency Data.
briefing.example: One refill stream, two buckets, three colors.
simplifications: Crates stand for packets; shipping labels stand for packet fields and application identity.
Time advances in fixed ticks. Traffic traces do not react to loss.
Belts add one tick per grid tile; factory geometry is a teaching metaphor.
Output docks can accept the whole burst; these lessons isolate metering from output congestion.
Token buckets begin full. Refill is exact to whole bytes; sub-byte credit is retained.
briefing.plain_language: A cascade has a main bucket and an overflow bucket. A crate is green if the main bucket can pay, yellow if only the overflow bucket can pay, and red if neither can pay.

wrong-mark.why_wrong: The yellow lane uses the green codepoint. The meter color must choose the corresponding AF2x marking.
wrong-mark.concept_reinforced: One refill stream, two buckets, three colors.

hints.text: Green spends committed tokens. Yellow spends excess tokens. Red spends neither.
Committed tokens refill first; only their overflow fills the excess bucket.
Mark green AF21, yellow AF22 and red AF23. The suffix is drop precedence, not another service class.

guide: Predict the fixed 1000 B/s cascade: CBS 1500, EBS 3000.
Paint the three output lanes AF21 (18), AF22 (20), AF23 (22).
Red is a color here; this work order delivers all three colors.

title: Twin Towers
concept: Respect trusted colors; measure untrusted traffic afresh.

briefing.title: Twin Towers
briefing.explanation: trTCM independently fills peak and committed buckets; red fails peak, yellow spends peak only, green spends both. Color-aware trTCM cannot upgrade yellow to green or red to another color. trTCM requires PIR >= CIR and positive PBS/CBS, with rates in bytes per second and burst sizes in bytes. RFC 4594 recommends preserving trusted color marking with aware meters and using blind meters when marking is not trusted or preserved. RFC 4594 recommends trTCM and AF41/AF42/AF43 for Multimedia Conferencing.
briefing.example: Respect trusted colors; measure untrusted traffic afresh.
simplifications: Crates stand for packets; shipping labels stand for packet fields and application identity.
Time advances in fixed ticks. Traffic traces do not react to loss.
Belts add one tick per grid tile; factory geometry is a teaching metaphor.
Output docks can accept the whole burst; these lessons isolate metering from output congestion.
Token buckets begin full. Refill is exact to whole bytes; sub-byte credit is retained.
briefing.plain_language: The two tanks measure different limits: peak and committed rate. A trusted color is a previous measurement you must respect. An untrusted color is a claim you measure again.

wrong-meter-mode.why_wrong: The trusted path ignores the incoming color and may upgrade traffic that was already marked yellow or red.
wrong-meter-mode.concept_reinforced: Respect trusted colors; measure untrusted traffic afresh.

hints.text: Peak and committed tokens refill independently.
An aware meter never upgrades an incoming yellow or red crate.
Use aware on the trusted lane and blind on the untrusted lane. Both use PIR 4000, PBS 3000, CIR 1000, CBS 1500.

guide: Predict the fixed tanks: trusted aware, user blind.
Change the editable trusted tank to aware and the user tank to blind.
The three paint lanes are already prepared as AF41, AF42 and AF43.

title: Express Lane
concept: Protect priority service without starving the shared lane.

briefing.title: Express Lane
briefing.explanation: RFC 4594 recommends policing EF traffic to protect the network and providing low-delay service. A scheduler gates departures according to a service discipline; DiffServ PHBs do not mandate a single scheduling algorithm. RFC 4594 recommends priority queuing for Telephony and rate queuing for the other listed service classes.
briefing.example: Protect priority service without starving the shared lane.
simplifications: Crates stand for packets; shipping labels stand for packet fields and application identity.
Time advances in fixed ticks. Traffic traces do not react to loss.
Belts add one tick per grid tile; factory geometry is a teaching metaphor.
Token buckets begin full. Refill is exact to whole bytes; sub-byte credit is retained.
briefing.plain_language: An express lane only helps if its entry is controlled. Otherwise a flood can occupy it continuously. Repair the voice policer and watch the web queue begin to move.

unpoliced-priority.why_wrong: The oversized policer admits a priority flood, taking capacity needed by the shared lane.
unpoliced-priority.concept_reinforced: Protect priority service without starving the shared lane.

hints.text: The priority queue is served whenever it has an eligible crate.
A flood can keep that queue full. Police before the queue, not after it.
The voice contract is 1000 B/s with a 1000-byte burst. The web lane needs 20,000 bytes during the measurement window.

guide: Set policer to 1000 B/s and a 1000-byte burst.
Run the trace and compare delivered web bytes with its 20,000-byte goal.
Inspect one voice crate to see its queue delay.

title: Shares
concept: Share output bytes among queues, including Default.

briefing.title: Shares
briefing.explanation: A scheduler gates departures according to a service discipline; DiffServ PHBs do not mandate a single scheduling algorithm. RFC 4594 requires the Standard Default Forwarding service class; other service classes are optional. RFC 4594 recommends priority queuing for Telephony and rate queuing for the other listed service classes.
briefing.example: Share output bytes among queues, including Default.
simplifications: Crates stand for packets; shipping labels stand for packet fields and application identity.
Time advances in fixed ticks. Traffic traces do not react to loss.
Belts add one tick per grid tile; factory geometry is a teaching metaphor.
briefing.plain_language: Think of the weights as turns in a shared loading schedule. A weight of three receives more byte credit than a weight of one. No queue should disappear from the schedule.

class-starved.why_wrong: The video weight takes too much of the finite congestion window. Backup or Default misses its required byte budget.
class-starved.concept_reinforced: Share output bytes among queues, including Default.

hints.text: Weights buy byte service, not packet-count quotas.
The Default queue must remain reachable and have a positive weighted share.
Try the planned 3:2:1 allocation for video, backup and web. Check bytes before the congestion window closes.

guide: Select merge and set video 3, backup 2, web 1.
Keep the Default marker at DSCP 0.
Run and inspect the measured bytes in the congestion window.

title: Spillway
concept: Drop higher AF drop precedence sooner as the queue grows.

briefing.title: Spillway
briefing.explanation: RFC 4594 Figure 4 lists no AQM for EF, CS5, CS4 and CS3. For Multimedia Conferencing, RFC 4594 specifies loss probability AF41 no greater than AF42, no greater than AF43. RFC 4594 orders AF4 RED thresholds: min43 < max43 <= min42 < max42 <= min41 < max41, with max41 within assigned queue memory. RFC 4594 describes RED dropping or ECN-marking all arrivals above a maximum threshold; this game models drops, instantaneous depth, and deterministic spacing.
briefing.example: Drop higher AF drop precedence sooner as the queue grows.
simplifications: Crates stand for packets; shipping labels stand for packet fields and application identity.
Time advances in fixed ticks. Traffic traces do not react to loss.
Belts add one tick per grid tile; factory geometry is a teaching metaphor.
Queue depth is instantaneous, not averaged.
Drops use exact deterministic spacing, not random sampling.
Measured loss on this finite trace does not prove a stochastic loss-probability guarantee.
briefing.plain_language: A Spillway starts discarding selected crates before its queue fills. Within AF4, the third drop-precedence color must be treated more harshly than the first.

thresholds-overlap.why_wrong: AF43 continues into AF42’s dropping range because its maximum is above AF42’s minimum.
thresholds-overlap.concept_reinforced: Drop higher AF drop precedence sooner as the queue grows.

aqm-on-ef.why_wrong: The voice path reaches a Spillway. RFC 4594 recommends against AQM for the Telephony service class.
aqm-on-ef.concept_reinforced: Drop higher AF drop precedence sooner as the queue grows.

hints.text: AF43 starts dropping first, then AF42, then AF41.
The maximum threshold of AF43 must not exceed the minimum of AF42.
Keep EF, CS5, CS4 and CS3 on the ordinary Buffer Belt. The intended AF ranges are 10–20, 20–30 and 30–40.

guide: Change AF43 maximum from 25 to 20.
Keep the protected traffic on the ordinary buffer.
Run and compare offered/dropped counts for all three AF4 markings.

title: Rush Hour
concept: Bring nine service classes through one busy enterprise hop.

briefing.title: Rush Hour
briefing.explanation: RFC 4594 Example 3 has Network Control, OAM, Standard, Telephony, Signaling, Multimedia Conferencing, Multimedia Streaming, High-Throughput Data and Low-Priority Data. RFC 5865 adds Admitted Telephony and capacity admission guidance for three video classes; the game does not simulate admission control. RFC 8622 updates RFC 4594 to recommend LE (000001) for Low-Priority Data instead of the prior CS1 recommendation. RFC 4594 recommends policing EF traffic to protect the network and providing low-delay service. RFC 4594 recommends CS6 for routing/control, reserves CS7 for possible future control use, and excludes user traffic from Network Control treatment. RFC 4594 Figure 4 lists no AQM for EF, CS5, CS4 and CS3. For Multimedia Conferencing, RFC 4594 specifies loss probability AF41 no greater than AF42, no greater than AF43. RFC 4594 orders AF4 RED thresholds: min43 < max43 <= min42 < max42 <= min41 < max41, with max41 within assigned queue memory. RFC 4594 describes RED dropping or ECN-marking all arrivals above a maximum threshold; this game models drops, instantaneous depth, and deterministic spacing.
briefing.example: Bring nine service classes through one busy enterprise hop.
simplifications: Crates stand for packets; shipping labels stand for packet fields and application identity.
Time advances in fixed ticks. Traffic traces do not react to loss.
Belts add one tick per grid tile; factory geometry is a teaching metaphor.
This is the historical nine-class RFC 4594 Example 3. RFC 8622 replaces its CS1 Low Priority mapping with LE (DSCP 1); LE behavior is outside this version.
RFC 5865 admission control is not simulated.
Queue depth is instantaneous; drop spacing is deterministic; no sender feedback is simulated.
Conferencing arrives already classified and colored at a trusted boundary.
Weights, capacities and rate contracts are this work order’s teaching values, not universal RFC configuration values.
Token buckets begin full. Refill is exact to whole bytes; sub-byte credit is retained.
briefing.plain_language: This is the full factory. Two settings are deliberately wrong: the voice limit is too large, and the AF43 dropping range overlaps AF42. Repair them, then use the checks to verify the whole hop.

untrusted-mark.why_wrong: The untrusted Default path still carries a control marking after its marker.
untrusted-mark.concept_reinforced: Bring nine service classes through one busy enterprise hop.

missing-standard.why_wrong: Default traffic is being marked as another class, so the factory has no dedicated reachable DF queue.
missing-standard.concept_reinforced: Bring nine service classes through one busy enterprise hop.

unpoliced-priority.why_wrong: The voice flood exceeds the work-order contract but is admitted to the strict-priority input.
unpoliced-priority.concept_reinforced: Bring nine service classes through one busy enterprise hop.

hints.text: Follow the access path: classify the application, mark, then queue.
Repair the voice contract before the priority queue. Keep an independent DF queue.
Use 2000 B/s and a 1000-byte voice burst. Correct the AF43 maximum to 20, then inspect every remaining check.

guide: Set policer to 2000 B/s and burst 1000 bytes.
Set q-conferencing AF43 maximum to 20.
Run all checks. This same verified factory powers the presentation demo.
